summary: Israeli prime minister whose direct engagement with American presidents, Congress and U.S. advocacy organizations has shaped debates over military aid, Iran, Jerusalem and the Gaza war. He has addressed joint meetings of Congress four times—more than any other foreign dignitary—while cultivating alliances and public disputes across successive U.S. administrations.

chapters.title: Congress as a political arena
chapters.dek: Four joint-meeting addresses gave Netanyahu an unusual platform inside American politics.
chapters.body: Netanyahu addressed joint meetings of Congress in 1996, 2011, 2015 and 2024, more often than any other foreign dignitary [[house-addresses]]. The repeated invitations made Congress an independent arena for his relationship with the United States, not merely an audience for bilateral diplomacy.

chapters.title: Iran and the Obama break
chapters.dek: The 2015 speech turned a policy dispute into an American partisan confrontation.
chapters.body: Netanyahu's March 2015 address argued against the emerging nuclear agreement with Iran while the Obama administration defended the agreement as the strongest available restraint on Iran's nuclear program [[govinfo-2015, obama-iran]]. The dispute strained political relations without ending military and intelligence cooperation [[obama-meeting]].

chapters.title: Aid beyond personal conflict
chapters.dek: Institutional security cooperation outlasted disputes between leaders.
chapters.body: In September 2016 the two governments concluded a ten-year assistance memorandum covering FY2019 through FY2028. It committed $33 billion in Foreign Military Financing and additional missile-defense support, producing the commonly cited $38 billion framework [[mou-2016, state-security]]. The agreement is U.S. government assistance to Israel, not money paid to Netanyahu.

chapters.title: The Trump alignment
chapters.dek: Jerusalem, the Golan Heights, Iran and normalization brought the two leaders together.
chapters.body: Netanyahu publicly praised Trump's recognition decisions and withdrawal from the Iran nuclear agreement [[trump-plan, trump-golan]]. The 2020 Abraham Accords added diplomatic normalization between Israel and Arab states to that alignment [[abraham-accords]].

chapters.title: Gaza and the Biden years
chapters.dek: Security support and public disagreement existed at the same time.
chapters.body: Netanyahu returned to Congress in July 2024 during the Gaza war. The invitation, attendance disputes and speech showed both the depth of congressional support and the widening American disagreement over the conduct and duration of the war [[govinfo-2024, crs-israel]].

chapters.title: The U.S. advocacy relationship
chapters.dek: AIPAC connects congressional politics to the bilateral relationship but remains a distinct American institution.
chapters.body: In January 2026 Netanyahu met a bipartisan congressional delegation organized by AIPAC and thanked its members for supporting Israel [[aipac-delegation-2026]]. AIPAC, its PAC and United Democracy Project are American organizations with their own legal records; their spending must not be presented as Netanyahu's personal money.

chapters.title: Alliance and dependence
chapters.dek: The relationship with Trump remained politically valuable but no longer eliminated policy conflict.
chapters.body: Reporting in 2026 described disagreements over Iran, Lebanon and Gaza alongside continued political support. Trump ultimately endorsed Netanyahu for reelection, illustrating both the value of the American relationship and the risk to Netanyahu when the two leaders diverged [[reuters-iran-2026, ap-trump-2026]].
